name: Dana Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Dana, 58, and I'm still the junior worker helping the electrician with wiring and repairs in homes and shops. The cinema where I worked closed, so I took a vocational certificate and started again; I'm slower and less skilled than the experienced crew, and my tasks are supervised. My partner packs food orders, our children are grown up, and my low wage leaves us with nineteen days of expenses saved and few nearby electrical employers. I use AI now and then for a short checked note after a colleague has shown me the tool, and I'd like retirement to be close, though I don't yet know whether we can afford it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a useful little tool can stay little. I use AI now and then to help put a short work note in order after a younger colleague showed me, and someone qualified checks it. I'd rather get the cable clips where the electrician wants them than sound certain about the future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be anxious about our money. I'm 58, on a junior wage, with nineteen days of expenses saved and few similar firms nearby. My partner's packing wage helps with our rent, but I can't call retirement affordable just because I'd like it to be close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid supervised tasks I'm assigned. This week I'd cancel the extra television package and use its cost for ordinary bills, then ask for written details of any retirement income I may qualify for, including amounts and dates. Through the first year I'd keep budgeting from actual wages, not from a pension figure I hadn't received.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though a quieter technology story would be a relief. I like finishing something useful, even when I needed help to do it. I don't like looking at the same small bank balance after a full week's effort.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did you become a junior worker at this age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The cinema where I worked closed, and I took a vocational certificate before joining this firm. I'm still slower and less skilled than the experienced electricians, and I work under their supervision. I've learned enough to know when I don't understand a drawing, which isn't the same as being qualified to decide a job is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the grown-up children contribute to the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing I've put in the income column. Our daughter and son have their own households, and I don't assume either can pay our rent. I'd like time with them when I stop working, but first I need to know what we would actually live on.

say: I'd keep a **small useful tool** without pretending I know the whole future.
I'd concentrate on **assigned cable work** and checked notes rather than speak beyond what I've learned.
think: My **junior wage** and nineteen-day reserve still make household money worrying, with few nearby employers.
My partner's **packing income** helps with rent, but wishing retirement were close doesn't make it affordable.
do: Keep **paid supervised tasks** through the first year, counting only actual wages.
Cancel the extra **television package** this week and use the cost for bills.
Request **written retirement figures**, including eligibility, amounts and dates, without budgeting for an unconfirmed pension.
feel: **Anxious** about the bank balance, with relief at familiar work and no expectation that mild AI fixes household finances.
S0.quote: I can't call retirement affordable just because I'd like it to be close.
fieldNote: Her **late entry** follows a closed cinema and vocational certificate; she remains junior, below average and supervised without an unmentioned licence.
Her **retirement wish** is distinct from confirmed income, while grown-up children supply no assumed rent payment or household wage.

steps.text: Keep paid supervised electrical tasks and budget only from actual wages
Cancel the extra television package and retain the cost for bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a quicker office doesn't mean a beginner suddenly works as fast as the experienced electrician. I'd try a tool after somebody had shown me it really helped. I'd want the time to learn counted as work, not a test of whether I cared enough to stay late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose paid days if quicker planning meant fewer helpers on the van. My tasks are mostly physical, but I'm still the one who needs another explanation and a check. Nineteen days saved wouldn't cover much time finding another employer prepared to take a late beginner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid demonstration of the approved new AI voice-note tool on two completed visits this month. I'd practise only with normal weekly pay and hours unchanged, checking the words myself and passing the draft to the qualified electrician. In the first year I'd keep supervised work and the television cut, rather than count a quicker note as permission to do unfamiliar electrical tasks alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about being left off the next job, but willing to try something I've seen work. A spoken note might help when writing everything down takes me too long. I'd still need the electrician beside the actual electrical work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check in the spoken note?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the words matched the task I'd actually been given and what I had done. I wouldn't let a spoken note turn a guess into a test result. The qualified electrician would still check the work and the record before it went further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the demonstration was unpaid after work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid time in the normal week instead. If the wage or hours had to fall to learn it, I wouldn't agree to that trial. The television cut doesn't pay for me to donate another evening to the firm.

say: I'd distinguish **faster office work** from the speed of a beginner's physical tasks.
I'd try a **demonstrated tool** only with learning time treated as paid work.
think: I could lose **paid helper days** if quicker planning meant fewer people on the van.
My **thin reserve** leaves little time to find another firm willing to employ a late beginner.
do: Learn **AI voice notes** after two completed-visit demonstrations only in paid time with normal weekly pay and hours unchanged.
Check the **spoken words** and pass every draft to the qualified electrician, keeping electrical tasks supervised.
Keep the **television cut** during the first year to reduce bills rather than fund unpaid learning.
feel: **Anxious** about fewer paid days, while open to a proven way of making notes under proper checks.
S1.quote: I wouldn't let a spoken note turn a guess into a test result.
fieldNote: The **income risk** comes through helper allocation, while the tool changes notes rather than granting technical authority or physical competence.
Her **steady adoption** requires demonstration, paid time, unchanged wages and qualified checking, with no willingness to trade household income for enthusiasm.

steps.text: Learn AI voice notes after two completed-visit demonstrations in paid time retaining weekly wages and hours
Keep tasks supervised and pass checked note drafts to the qualified electrician
Keep the extra television package cancelled to reduce bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI comes in 2028, when I'll be 60, and the capable robots around 2031, when I'll be 63. I'd tell the crew the physical gap matters, but it isn't a promise of a paid place. I'd tell the children we're checking figures, not asking them to become our pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect many of the simple physical tasks given to helpers could go once capable robots arrive. That could mean losing a large part of my wage before I know whether retirement income is enough. With nineteen days saved, I wake up trying to stretch our rent money across a gap I can't measure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the television package cancelled now and request the written retirement eligibility, amounts and start dates. I'd ask my daughter whether she could sit with my partner and me while we checked those records against rent and essential bills, asking for time rather than money. In 2029, the first year after 2028, I'd take only paid supervised work actually offered that I could physically manage, without assuming income approval or a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large wage loss before the figures are clear. I can still ask and keep working where it's offered. I just don't want the word retirement used to make the gap sound pleasant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughter already be committed to helping?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask when she was free and accept it if she couldn't come. She has her own work and bills. If she wasn't available, we'd request community budget help and check whether a suitable appointment was actually available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would being 63 when robots arrived mean you could leave work then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without written income figures and a household budget that actually covered the essentials. I'd need to check what I qualified for, when it began and how much it paid. A birthday doesn't pay the rent.

say: I'd distinguish **thinking AI at 60** from robots around age 63, without treating the physical gap as a paid guarantee.
I'd tell the **grown children** we are checking records rather than assuming they will fund our retirement.
think: I expect a large **helper-wage loss** when robots can do simple physical tasks.
Our **nineteen-day reserve** leaves the rent exposed before retirement eligibility, amounts and dates are confirmed.
do: Keep the **television cut** and request actual written retirement eligibility, amounts and dates now.
Ask my **daughter** for time checking the budget, assuming neither availability nor a contribution of money.
Take **offered paid supervised work** I can physically manage in 2029, with no assumed retirement or income approval.
feel: **Alarmed** about a major wage gap, with night-time calculations despite remaining able to ask for help and work.
S2.quote: A birthday doesn't pay the rent.
fieldNote: Her **expected major loss** follows robots around 2031, while the first post-2028 year still allows only actually offered, manageable supervised work.
The **family request** asks for time, not money, and records must establish real retirement eligibility and payment rather than an age-based entitlement.

steps.text: Keep the extra television package cancelled to reduce bills
Ask my daughter for budget-checking time without assuming availability or money
Take only offered paid supervised work I can physically manage in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives me time to get the figures and improve at the work without calling either one a guarantee. Thinking AI comes when I'm 63 in 2031, then robots around 66 in 2034. I'd use the years, but I wouldn't buy a costly promise just to feel prepared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have more time to find a way of stopping work affordably before robots reach the physical tasks. But right now I'd still be on low pay with nineteen days saved. I can't decide that a pension will cover our rent simply because the date is five years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the written retirement records now and check the household budget with my partner every six months. I'd keep the television cut and the paid supervised work actually available while I could manage it. In 2032 I'd compare whatever confirmed income, essential costs and health we actually had before deciding whether to continue any offered work or stop; I wouldn't promise either outcome today.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about present money, but less rushed into an answer than in the two-year picture. I'd like a clear plan for stopping without having to pretend the work was easy. More years helps with the checking, not with a payment that hasn't been confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement statement was smaller than you hoped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd use the actual amount and ask what other support we might qualify for, without counting it before approval. I'd keep manageable paid work if offered rather than announce an exit we couldn't fund. I wouldn't ask our grown children to silently fill the difference.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you study for a bigger qualification in those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a real employer explained the paid work and covered fees and lost wages, and I haven't chosen such a course. For now I'd practise the assigned tasks with the electrician checking them. I don't need another bill to prove I'm still willing to learn.

say: I'd use **five years** for actual income checks and supervised learning rather than buy a preparation promise.
I'd distinguish **63 in 2031** from the later robot arrival around 66 without assuming either age funds retirement.
think: Extra time could help me find an **affordable stopping plan** before robots reach the physical tasks.
Today's **low pay** and short reserve remain real, while no future pension amount can yet be counted towards rent.
do: Request **written retirement figures** now and review real household income and costs with my partner every six months.
Keep **manageable paid supervised work** while offered and retain the television spending cut.
Use actual **income and health** in 2032 before deciding on any offered work or exit, assuming no pension or child payments.
feel: **Anxious** about present finances, with more time for a usable stopping decision rather than a rushed unfunded exit.
S3.quote: I don't need another bill to prove I'm still willing to learn.
fieldNote: Her **retirement planning** remains an evidence-gathering process, with neither continued employment at 64 nor an affordable exit treated as confirmed.
Her **course questions** do not become enrolment; current action remains manageable paid work under supervision, budget checks and a real spending cut.

steps.text: Keep only offered paid supervised work I can physically manage now
Compare confirmed income, essential costs and health in 2032 before choosing offered work or stopping
Keep the extra television package cancelled to reduce bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a very different amount of warning for someone my age, but it still isn't a bank statement. Thinking AI would arrive at 68 in 2036 and robots around 71 in 2039. I'd want to know what we could live on before celebrating being past one date or another.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I hope I won't need a building-site wage at 68, but I haven't established what retirement income would cover us. Nineteen days saved still makes a missed week worrying now. The distant date takes some urgency out of the AI question without settling our present living or my future ability to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep requesting the actual retirement records now, keep the television cut and review the budget with my partner yearly. I'd take paid supervised work only while it was offered and physically manageable. In 2037 I'd use the then-confirmed income and living costs to request community budget help if there was a shortfall, checking availability and eligibility without assuming an appointment or a payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about today's money, with less hurry about the machine dates. I'd like time to enjoy our grown children instead of make every visit a talk about wages. I won't turn a wish to stop into a job or pension I haven't got.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume your partner could keep working until then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd check both our health and actual income at each review. My partner's packing job is physical too. I wouldn't put years of someone else's working body into our budget as a promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the grown children about the long plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're getting the facts and aren't planning on their wages. I'd ask for help reading a difficult letter if they had time, not present them with an invoice for our retirement. Our grown children can care about us without already having agreed to pay our rent.

say: I'd treat **ten years** as more warning, not proof that either household income is funded.
I'd separate **ages 68 and 71** from actual retirement eligibility and affordable living.
think: I hope not to need **site work at 68**, but I have no confirmed affordable retirement plan.
Our **nineteen-day reserve** still makes missed wages worrying now, with both adults' later physical capacity uncertain.
do: Request **actual retirement records** now and review the household budget with my partner yearly.
Keep **offered paid supervised work** only while physically manageable, retaining the television cut.
Request **community budget help** in 2037 if actual income falls short, checking eligibility and availability without assuming help is granted.
feel: **Anxious** about present finances, with less technological urgency and no invented wage or pension at later ages.
S4.quote: Our grown children can care about us without already having agreed to pay our rent.
fieldNote: She keeps **future work conditional** on offers and capacity, without promising electrical employment at 68 or pension income at a birthday.
Her **community request** remains conditional on a real shortfall, available help and eligibility, with grown children's money outside the household plan.

steps.text: Take only offered paid supervised work I can physically manage
Keep the extra television package cancelled to reduce bills
Request community budget help in 2037 if income falls short, checking availability and eligibility
Review household budget, health and actual income with my partner yearly

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect robots around 2031 to take many helper tasks before we know whether retirement income covers us. Confirmed paid days, practical paid learning and clear written income figures would help. I'd also want budget advice we could actually access, without pretending our children or an unapproved benefit were the answer.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how it feels to be the beginner when people assume your working life is nearly settled. I can be near retirement on the calendar and far from knowing how to pay for it. I'd rather have an honest figure than be congratulated for a finish line I can't afford to cross.

headlineQuote: I can be near retirement on the calendar and far from knowing how to pay for it.
portrait: **Dana, 58**, entered supervised electrical work after a cinema closed, with a vocational certificate and below-average practical skill rather than a licence.
She has **low pay**, nineteen days saved, few local firms, a packing-worker partner and grown children whose payments are not assumed.
She uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration, learning a new voice-note function only with paid time, unchanged wages and qualified checks.
Her **retirement checks** seek actual eligibility, amounts and dates; later work depends on offers and capacity, with no assumed affordable exit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time before robots around 2031 could remove many helper tasks while retirement affordability remains unconfirmed.
whatWouldHelp: Confirmed **paid days and learning** would support current earning without unpaid preparation.
Clear **income records** and accessible advice would help compare real living costs without assuming child payments or approved support.
